title: Ah! Sun-flower: date and plate
short: From Songs of Experience (1794), where Blake etched it on one plate with 'My Pretty Rose Tree' and 'The Lilly'; Blake's title is 'Ah! Sun-flower'.
body: The poem's three companions on a single plate are all flower poems about desire, jealousy and restraint. Blake's own title and spelling are 'Ah! Sun-flower'; the archive's text normalises them. The poem has two quatrains of mainly anapaestic trimeter, rhymed abab. The opening 'Ah' can be read as sympathy, or weariness, or longing, and the sentence is incomplete: the whole poem is a single sentence, an address to the flower whose main verb, 'Arise', is held back until the seventh line, which suits its theme of desire that never arrives. The flower is 'weary of time' because it is bound to the sun's daily course.

sources.cite: The William Blake Archive (ed. M. Eaves, R. N. Essick, J. Viscomi): illuminated copies
David V. Erdman, ed., The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (rev. ed., 1982), text and commentary by Harold Bloom
Geoffrey Keynes, ed., Songs of Innocence and of Experience (Oxford UP, 1970), introduction and commentary

anchor: countest the steps of the sun
title: Counting the sun's steps: Clytie
short: The sunflower turns to follow the sun, as in Ovid's myth of Clytie, who pined for Apollo and became a flower that always faces him.
body: In Metamorphoses 4, the nymph Clytie, abandoned by the Sun, sits on the ground nine days watching his course until she becomes a flower (the heliotrope) that still turns towards him. Later tradition identified the flower with the sunflower. Blake's flower 'countest the steps of the sun', measuring time by its motion: devotion becomes slavery to time. The image combines natural observation (heliotropism) with the classical emblem of unrequited love.

sources.cite: Ovid, Metamorphoses 4.256-270 (Clytie)
S. Foster Damon, A Blake Dictionary (1965)
'Ah! Sun-flower', Wikipedia

title: The golden clime
short: The 'golden clime' (region) is where the sun sets, the West: a heaven or paradise where the 'traveller's journey is done'.
body: 'Clime' means a region or zone. The sunset west has long been the place of the Hesperides and the Isles of the Blessed, and in Christian imagery of heaven. The traveller whose 'journey is done' suggests life's pilgrimage ending in death. Blake's irony, as many readers see it, is that this heaven is only another form of the sunflower's endless longing: it is defined by being always elsewhere.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v.
David V. Erdman, ed., The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (rev. ed., 1982), text and commentary by Harold Bloom
Harold Bloom, Blake's Apocalypse (1963)

title: The traveller's journey
short: The traveller whose journey ends recalls the Christian pilgrim of Hebrews and Bunyan, for whom life is a road to the heavenly country.
body: Hebrews 11:13-16 calls the faithful 'strangers and pilgrims on the earth' who seek 'a better country, that is, an heavenly'. Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress (1678), which Blake later illustrated, makes the journey to the Celestial City the plot of a Christian life. Blake's line keeps the comfort of that idea but places it in the sunflower's longing gaze: rest is imagined at the sunset, the point where the day's journey, and life itself, ends. The quiet monosyllables of 'is done' give the line a dying fall.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Hebrews 11:13-16; Revelation 14:4
John Bunyan, The Pilgrim's Progress (1678), the Land of Beulah and the Celestial City
David V. Erdman, ed., The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (rev. ed., 1982), text and commentary by Harold Bloom

title: The pale virgin shrouded in snow
short: A woman who died a virgin, her chastity figured as a cold white shroud: snow as an emblem of frigidity and denial.
body: White and snow are traditional emblems of virginity (compare the virgins who follow the Lamb in Revelation 14:4). Blake turns the emblem cold: the virgin is 'pale' and 'shrouded', so her purity is a kind of death in life. In the companion poems on the same plate, 'My Pretty Rose Tree' and 'The Lilly', Blake also explores refusal and jealousy in love; Some commentators read the three poems on the plate as a group about the costs of restraint. 'Shrouded' also means hidden: her desire is concealed even from herself.

sources.cite: The Bible, Authorized (King James) Version, Revelation 14:4
S. Foster Damon, A Blake Dictionary (1965)
David V. Erdman, ed., The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (rev. ed., 1982), text and commentary by Harold Bloom

anchor: the Youth pined away with desire
title: The Youth and the pale Virgin
short: The Youth who 'pined away with desire' and the 'pale virgin shrouded in snow' are figures of repressed sexuality who denied themselves in hope of heaven.
body: The Youth's wasting recalls the lovelorn figures of pastoral and Ovidian tradition, and the virgin 'shrouded in snow' suggests a chaste death, her shroud the whiteness of virginity and frigidity. In Blake's Songs of Experience, sexual restraint imposed by religion and morality is a recurrent target ('Thou shalt not' writ over the door in 'The Garden of Love'). These figures 'Arise from their graves' and aspire to the same place as the sunflower: Blake suggests that their heaven is the sublimated form of their denied desire.

sources.cite: David V. Erdman, ed., The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (rev. ed., 1982), text and commentary by Harold Bloom
Harold Bloom, Blake's Apocalypse (1963)
William Blake, 'The Garden of Love', Songs of Experience (1794)

anchor: Arise from their graves, and aspire
title: Arise ... and aspire
greek: Latin aspirare, to breathe upon, strive toward
short: 'Arise' and 'aspire' may describe a resurrection, or express a wish, or command; the grammar is open, and so is the poem's attitude.
body: Grammatically 'Arise' could be indicative (they arise), subjunctive (where they may arise), or imperative. 'Aspire' combines rising (Latin aspirare, to strive upward) with ambition. Readers divide: some take the poem as a sympathetic picture of longing for transcendence; many others take it as an ironic critique, since the dead 'arise' only into another longing. The final line, 'Where my Sunflower wishes to go', ends with wishing, not arriving, and the speaker's 'my' implies that he shares the desire he describes.

sources.cite: Harold Bloom, Blake's Apocalypse (1963)
David V. Erdman, ed., The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (rev. ed., 1982), text and commentary by Harold Bloom
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v.

anchor: Where my Sunflower wishes to go
title: Desire deferred
short: The poem's circular structure ends where it began, with the flower's wish: unfulfilled desire becomes a state of being.
body: The repeated 'Where' (ll. 4, 5, 8) ties the poem into a loop. It is often read alongside Blake's proverb in The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, 'He who desires but acts not, breeds pestilence'. In 1948 the poet Allen Ginsberg reported a visionary experience in Harlem of hearing Blake's voice reciting this poem, which he later described often; it is one example of the poem's influence on the Beat poets.

sources.cite: William Blake, The Marriage of Heaven and Hell (c. 1790), 'Proverbs of Hell'
David V. Erdman, ed., The Complete Poetry and Prose of William Blake (rev. ed., 1982), text and commentary by Harold Bloom
'Ah! Sun-flower', Wikipedia (reception, including Ginsberg)
